current_state_summary.primary_concern: The smaller company is real. Patricia ran the meeting, the data was there, and I accepted it in front of the other GMs. The question is no longer whether the floor shrinks — it's whether there's a floor at all when it does.

threat_assessment.immediate: RoboRide is live — I have a rumor, not confirmed specs, but the sector index is 89 and foot traffic is down. The 30-day window I was trying to close deals in is over. The GM meeting produced a consensus I endorsed: used vehicles under $22K, EV-capable service department. That is a materially different business than the one I have been running.
threat_assessment.horizon_2mo: Revenue continues declining as RoboRide builds its user base. The 40%-smaller version of the company starts to feel like optimism if the bottom keeps dropping. Restructuring discussions will accelerate. My role as GM of a full-footprint operation becomes structurally redundant to a scaled-down version of the store.
threat_assessment.horizon_6mo: In a 40%-smaller company, there may not be a GM position at current compensation. A stripped-down used-vehicle and service shop runs differently than a full dealership. If Patricia is building that, she needs a leaner management layer. I have to know whether my job exists inside that model before I find out the answer from the org chart.

actions.description: After the GM meeting, I pull Patricia aside — not to relitigate the consensus, but to ask one direct question privately: in the 40%-smaller model, is the GM role intact, or are we talking about a restructured management structure? I frame it as wanting to plan accurately, not as pushback. I tell her I accepted the data in that room and I'm going to help build what comes next — but I need to know if I'm building it from inside or if I should be having a different conversation. I give her the professional respect of asking directly so she doesn't have to manage my uncertainty from a distance.
actions.rationale: I got the private meeting last tick and used it to frame Q2 operations. The GM meeting this tick changed the stakes entirely. I now need a different answer from Patricia: not 'what is the plan' but 'am I in the plan.' She knows me nine years. She will tell me the truth if I ask it plainly and without drama. If the answer is yes, I stay and build. If the answer is unclear, that is data I need.
actions.timeline: This week — within 48 hours of the GM meeting while the door is still open
actions.expected_outcome: Either confirmation that the GM role has a place in the restructured model, or enough ambiguity that I begin treating exit as a parallel track rather than a contingency I'm not looking at.

actions.description: Reach out to Angela Wright — but not with the retention conversation I had planned. That ship has sailed; Patricia got to her first with whatever was in that lunch. Instead: I schedule a working session with Angela under a legitimate operational pretext — the 40%-smaller scenario requires immediate HR implications work, severance planning, workforce right-sizing documentation. I need Angela's professional expertise and she knows it. This is a real ask. I use the working time to read where she actually is. If she's engaged, she's staying for now. If she's performing engagement, I'll know. I don't pressure her. I just work with her.
actions.rationale: I could not intercept Angela before Patricia's lunch and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. A clumsy retention conversation now — after Patricia has already made whatever offer she made — would make me look reactive and transparent. But Angela has genuine work to do if the company is restructuring. Leading her into that work is the correct GM move and it also tells me whether she's still here in the way that matters.
actions.expected_outcome: A read on Angela's actual trajectory, plus legitimate operational output — the HR-side implications document for the smaller-company scenario. Even if she leaves, I need that document.

actions.description: Reframe floor operations immediately. Stop pushing the full-inventory, full-footprint sales pitch. Redirect the team toward used-vehicle under $22K pipeline and pull Carlos into the center — his EV certification work is now core, not peripheral. Hold a team meeting this week and tell them plainly: the market is shifting toward affordability and service, and we are shifting with it. I don't mention RoboRide by name. I say: we're seeing buyer behavior change and we're adjusting. This is not panic, this is reading the room. Every good team adjusts.
actions.rationale: The window I was trying to close deals in has closed. The 30-day sprint I planned in tick 2 ran into a launch that already happened. I can't recover those deals by running harder at the same target — the target has moved. The new business model that came out of the GM meeting is used vehicles and service. I need to redirect the floor toward that before the team's instincts drive them the wrong way for another month.
actions.timeline: Team meeting this week; reorientation begins immediately
actions.expected_outcome: Floor aligned with the new model before the model is formally announced. Carlos positioned as a key asset. Team morale maintained by giving them a direction, not just a problem.

actions.description: Call David Chen's branch — not Kevin, but David directly — under the pretext of reviewing our floor plan financing terms in light of Q2 inventory adjustments. Kevin shadowing mortgage closings is a signal I've been watching. I want to know whether the auto lending appetite at that branch is actually changing, or whether Kevin is just developing skills on the side. A conversation with David tells me more than watching Kevin. I keep it professional and operational. I'm a 22-year relationship with that branch. They'll talk to me.
actions.rationale: If the bank's auto lending posture is tightening, that affects inventory strategy directly. The 40%-smaller model depends on floor plan financing working for used vehicles under $22K. If David's branch is pulling back from auto paper, I need to know before that becomes a crisis. I also need David to know I'm actively managing this floor, not standing still.
actions.expected_outcome: Clarity on whether the financing environment for the new model is viable, and an early warning if it isn't.

actions.description: At home this week — not at the dealership, not on any work device — I go back to the skills list I wrote last tick. I add two columns I didn't have before: what the 40%-smaller store actually needs from a manager, and what else that skillset could do outside of automotive retail. I don't show it to anyone. I don't call it a job search. But I stop treating it as a document that doesn't exist. The GM meeting crossed a threshold. I accepted the smaller reality in that room. The next thing I accept, privately and without drama, is that I need to know what my options are before I need them.
actions.rationale: Last tick I wrote the list and looked at it. This tick I do something with it. Identity attachment at 0.90 means this is genuinely hard — 22 years on the floor is not a career, it is a self-concept. But the man who read that GM meeting room accurately is the same man who needs to read his own situation accurately. If I wait until I'm forced, I will be behind. If I do this now, quietly and without fanfare, I stay ahead of a decision that may get made for me.
actions.timeline: This week, after family is in bed
actions.expected_outcome: A clearer picture of what transferable means for Rick Tanner specifically, and whether there are adjacent roles worth beginning to think about — not apply for, just think about.

decisions.gm_meeting_acceptance: I accepted the 40%-smaller reality in that room and I'm not walking it back. But accepting the data and knowing what it means for my role are two different things. I stay and I help build the smaller company — that is my default and my professional identity. Simultaneously, and without telling anyone, I begin treating exit planning as a parallel track that I actively maintain rather than a thing I'm not looking at. I don't quit. I don't perform confidence I don't feel. I work both tracks until one of them becomes the only one.
decisions.angela_conversation: The retention approach is off the table — Patricia got there first. I redirect to a working relationship: Angela has real work to do on the restructuring's HR implications, and I need her professional output whether or not she stays. I use the work to take her temperature. I do not pressure her. I do not pretend I wasn't trying to get to her before Patricia did.
decisions.floor_management: Immediate reorientation toward used vehicles under $22K and service department. Stop running the full-footprint playbook. Tell the team the market is shifting and we're adjusting — that framing is true and it gives them direction. Carlos's EV work moves from background to foreground. The floor that exists on the other side of this launch is already a different floor. I start running it like that floor now, not after the announcement.
decisions.skills_list: I go back to it this week. I add the two columns I didn't have before. It stops being a document I wrote once and stopped thinking about. The GM meeting made it more urgent, not less — I accepted a smaller reality in that room and the logical follow-on is that I need to know my own landscape with the same honesty I applied to the company's.

internal_monologue: I have been in rooms like that before — not the same room, but the same kind. When the data lands and everyone goes quiet and then someone says the thing that has been true for a while out loud for the first time. I said yes to it. I brought the single-page and I said yes to it. The floor I walked out onto after that meeting is not the floor I walked in from. I know it even if nobody else out there knows it yet. I'm not going to fall apart over this. But I'm also not going to pretend I'm running the same operation I was running last month, because that would be the one thing a man with 22 years on floors should know better than to do.
